History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
• 40-year-old woman with acute continuous vertigo, nausea, and bilateral ear buzzing for the past ≈2 hours; assessment is labyrinthitis with symptomatic treatment initiated and in-person follow-up arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint – Sudden-onset dizziness described as “room spinning,” associated nausea, unsteadiness, and ear buzzing.  
• Onset & course – Began abruptly ~2 hours before consult while preparing breakfast; symptoms have been continuous.  
• Previous episode – Similar but milder event ≈1 month ago lasting 5–10 minutes and self-resolving.  
• Aggravating/relieving factors – None specifically identified; standing/walking feels unstable due to vertigo.  
• Associated symptoms – Nausea, shaky feeling, bilateral buzzing in ears.  
• Pertinent negatives – No limb weakness, no hearing loss, no ear pain or discharge, no recent viral illness (no cough/cold), no fever reported, no vomiting.  

Past Medical History:
• Premature ovarian failure – on hormone-replacement therapy (HRT).  
• No other chronic medical or surgical conditions noted.

Medications:
• Hormone-replacement therapy – specific preparation/dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• New prescription: medication name not captured (likely vestibular suppressant) – “1 tablet three times daily for 10 days” (dose/route otherwise not documented).

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Not discussed (smoking, alcohol, occupation, and lifestyle information not documented).

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• No physical exam performed in this telehealth visit; vitals not recorded.

Investigations:
• None to date.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected labyrinthitis (acute vertigo with ear buzzing, no focal neurologic deficits)  
  • Prescribe vestibular-suppressant medication (1 tab TID ×10 days).  
  • Arrange in-person appointment for otoscopic exam, blood pressure measurement, and gait assessment.  
  • Provide safety-net advice: if new limb weakness, severe headache, or persistent vomiting develops, proceed to Emergency Department (A&E).  

General Plan items:  
  • Patient instructed to contact support to book the in-person appointment.  
  • Medication can be taken with or without food; encourage adherence.  
  • Follow-up after in-person assessment to reassess diagnosis and treatment response.

Quality checks:
• Missing expected elements: vital signs, complete physical exam, detailed medication reconciliation, social and family history, exact name/dose of prescribed drug.  
• Internal conflicts: none noted.  
• Transcript quality: clear overall; occasional inaudible/omitted words (medication name not captured).
